documents.abstract: Proteomics is now generating unprecedented volumes of mass spectrometry data, driven by increasingly powerful instrumentation and large-scale studies. Yet our ability to translate these measurements into biological knowledge remains a major challenge. The limiting factor is no longer data generation, but our capacity to extract meaningful insights from increasingly complex molecular datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to reshape every stage of the proteomics workflow. Early applications focused on improving established computational approaches, where machine learning models enhanced conventional database search strategies by predicting peptide properties and improving peptide-spectrum match scoring. More recently, deep learning models are learning directly from tandem mass spectra for de novo peptide sequencing, enabling new discoveries. The next evolution will be AI-driven proteomics experiments, where models actively contribute to experimental decision-making. Rather than simply analyzing measurements after acquisition, AI could guide instruments toward collecting the most informative data, transforming proteomics from a strategy of measuring more toward one of measuring smarter. Ultimately, the greatest opportunity lies in moving beyond individual spectra and molecular identifications toward biological understanding. By integrating diverse omics measurements, AI may enable predictive representations of cellular systems and provide new ways to understand the complexity of life. I will explore the ongoing transformation of proteomics through AI: from models that enhance existing workflows, through systems that directly interpret molecular signals, toward intelligent technologies that could redefine how we perform experiments and uncover biological knowledge.

documents.abstract: Understanding human mobility during extreme flood events is critical for emergency evacuation and resilient transport planning, yet flood-induced behavioral heterogeneity remains difficult to characterize. Progress has been constrained by data scarcity and the inherent complexity of emergency decision-making, which often induces abnormal travel behaviors and anomalous mobility fluxes. We propose the Disaster-aware Trajectory Generator (DTG), integrating Large Language Model (LLM) agents into an agent-based framework to generate individual-level mobility trajectories under evolving urban flood conditions. Validated against 1.32 billion mobility records from the 2021 “7.20” Zhengzhou flood in China, DTG outperforms all traditional and LLM-enabled baselines, achieving a flood-induced inflow-shift prediction accuracy of 0.713 with outflow and OD distribution JSD of 0.069 and 0.047 during the disaster period. By combining accessibility-constrained disaster context reasoning with the representation of heterogeneous socio-demographic responses, DTG reveals critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and abnormal behavioral patterns, offering actionable insights for flood-resilient transport planning.

Artificial intelligence is transforming cognitive learning by reshaping pedagogical models and raising questions about its impact on higher-order thinking. AI-driven personalized learning improves knowledge acquisition, but its effect on creativity remains largely unexplored. Most research emphasizes content delivery over cognitive engagement, which leaves gaps in understanding how AI influences deeper learning processes. This study investigates how ChatGPT-enabled personalized learning, framed through Bloom’s Taxonomy, influences creative thinking among Indonesian higher education students, considering the moderating role of peer interaction. Using SEM via Smart-PLS 4.1, data from 533 Indonesian students reveal that personalized learning strengthens both lower-order cognitive skills—such as remembering, understanding, and applying—and higher-order functions, including analyzing, evaluating, and creating, which are essential for creativity. Among these, analyzing and creating have the strongest impact on creative thinking. Peer interaction selectively moderates this relationship, significantly enhancing creativity in tasks involving creation, while its effect on other cognitive functions remains limited. This study introduces a dynamic framework that integrates personalized learning, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and peer collaboration, offering new insights into how tailored cognitive processes and selective peer engagement drive creativity in learning environments.

Generative AI is now a routine presence in higher-education classrooms, shifting the operative question from whether to permit its use toward when and how access should be structured within a learning activity. This paper reports a design-based research programme examining phase-based AI constraints, deliberately restricting AI access to specific phases of a collaborative teaching method rather than permitting or prohibiting it wholesale, as a design principle for structuring human and AI contributions within collaborative learning activities. The wider DBR programme examined AI-augmented designs across six collaborative teaching methods, administered repeatedly to five student groups over two academic years; the phase-based AI-constraint principle reported here as DP1 was developed through, and its evidence anchored in, Think-Pair-Share, with the other five methods contributing broader DBR context rather than independent confirmatory evidence. Its strongest evidence comes from an AI-free Think phase within Think-Pair-Share, replicated across three independent student groups spanning three degree programs, where learners consistently endorsed the AI-free phase as appropriate; this endorsement pattern was typically the highest-scoring item on its questionnaire. This design itself resulted from an earlier design cycle within the same programme: an initial administration permitting AI access during this phase prompted redesign after the instructor's classroom observation indicated that independent reflection was being displaced by AI-mediated responses. We treat this endorsement as an empirical finding, not as a direct assessment of the quality or originality of what learners produced, and not as evidence that the phase in fact protects independent cognitive engagement; that stronger claim is a theoretically motivated proposition this study does not test, and we frame DP1 accordingly across three explicit levels: an empirical endorsement finding, a transferable design principle of differentiating AI access by activity phase rather than deciding it once for a whole activity, and an untested theoretical proposition about the cognitive mechanism this differentiation may support. A complementary, independent stakeholder strand surveyed higher-education professionals at a practitioner festival session, offering a modest, exploratory social-validity signal: the phase-based procedure itself was almost universally endorsed, while personal adoption intention was somewhat more reserved. An exploratory qualitative coding of practitioners' open responses showed only slight inter-coder reliability ( κ =0.17), so we do not use these responses to derive additional design principles, retaining only one response on function-based AI restriction as an illustrative example. The study is exploratory and formative, without a no-AI control condition or random assignment, and we frame its claims as design-principle evidence within a design-based research programme rather than as causal effect estimates. Anchored in independently replicated student endorsement data from Think-Pair-Share and supplemented by a practitioner social-validity signal, phase-based AI constraints offer higher-education instructors an actionable, low-friction design principle, one we expect to be conceptually transferable to other collaborative teaching methods, though this transfer remains to be empirically demonstrated.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: How are innovation inputs and measured outputs distributed across the regions of a resource-dependent post-Soviet economy, and how closely do they correspond? We use a balanced official panel of Kazakhstan’s 17 regions for 2014–2025 (204 region–year observations) covering four indicators: R&D expenditure, innovation-active enterprises, the innovation activity rate and innovative product output. Granted patents for inventions are available by region for 2021–2025 only; this series is shorter than the panel, so it is used in the 2025 cross-sectional and descriptive analyses and does not enter the panel or machine learning models. On the panel, we estimate dispersion measures, panel regression with region-clustered standard errors and tree-based machine learning interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations; on the 2025 cross-section, we compute correlations, clustering and spatial association statistics. Inputs are highly concentrated: Almaty and Astana together accounted for 65.1% of national R&D expenditure in 2025, and cross-regional dispersion did not narrow over the period. In the 2025 cross-section (n = 17), R&D expenditure, innovation-active enterprises and patent grants are strongly inter-correlated (r = 0.96–0.97), but none of the three is significantly correlated with innovative product output. This input–output misalignment is a pattern whose mechanisms we do not test. The panel specification has modest explanatory power (R2 = 0.188), which bounds the weight that can be placed on any single coefficient. Within it the innovation activity rate is the only significant predictor of output (β = 0.177, p < 0.001), an association that survives exclusion of the three regions affected by the 2022 administrative reform; because that indicator and the output measure are compiled within the same system of enterprise observation, it is reported as a within-dataset association requiring validation against independently measured indicators. Under region-grouped cross-validation, the machine learning models show no out-of-region predictive ability and are reported solely as in-sample interpretation. The contribution is a documented diagnosis of input–output misalignment in an understudied regional system, with an explicit account of what such data can and cannot support, and a prospective statement of what institutional readiness for algorithmic decision support in regional innovation policy would require.

This free sample edition contains two full chapters of "Reliable AI at Scale: Data Engineering for the Intelligent Systems Era," a book about the data systems artificial intelligence actually stands on. The book's argument: AI systems are data-intensive systems, and their failures are data failures. Included chapters: - Chapter 1: The Data-Intensive AI Stack — the book's thesis and the seven-layer frame (ingestion, storage, processing, orchestration, quality, observability, authority) every later chapter deepens. - Chapter 4: Stream Processing and Real-Time ML — event time, watermarks, and exactly-once semantics, then the ML turn: real-time features, point-in-time correctness, and training-serving skew. The full book has eleven chapters: 1. The Data-Intensive AI Stack 2. Ingestion at Scale: From Events to Actions 3. Storage for Intelligent Systems 4. Stream Processing and Real-Time ML 5. Consistency, Correctness, and Data Quality 6. Feature Engineering and Feature Platforms 7. Orchestration, Sagas, and Long-Running Workflows 8. Federated and Privacy-Preserving Learning 9. MLOps, Feedback Loops, and Continuous Intelligence 10. Autonomous Agents as Data-Intensive Systems 11. Operating AI Systems in Production: Reliability, Observability, Security Each chapter is written to stand alone: an opening production-failure scenario (a fictional composite), the principles that explain it, the architectural patterns that prevent it, trade-offs, and a "what to build first" checklist. About the author: Sai Prasad Veluru is a Senior Software Engineer at Immihub, where he works on distributed systems and production AI. Over eleven years in the industry — including engineering roles at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Visa — he has designed and operated high-throughput ingestion platforms, real-time streaming systems, and cloud-native data infrastructure, and he now builds agentic AI systems engineered to survive production. He is the author of twenty-five publications on distributed systems, stream processing, federated learning, and production AI, cited more than 150 times, and he serves as a judge at HackMIT and MHacks. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in qualitative data analysis, introducing reporting considerations not explicitly addressed by COREQ or SRQR. This study used a structured literature review–informed methodological synthesis to develop preliminary COREQ-AI and SRQR-AI extensions. Of 2,127 records identified, the synthesis included 65 studies. The proposed extensions address model specification, prompt transparency, algorithmic reflexivity, human-in-the-loop validation, AI auditability, data governance, and ethical accountability. Five independent researchers appraised the extensions; 80% considered them relevant and clear, 100% applicable, and 60% indicated that further refinement was needed. Illustrative applications further demonstrated their potential to identify AI-specific reporting information not captured by the original guidelines. COREQ-AI and SRQR-AI are preliminary, literature-informed reporting extensions intended to improve transparency and critical appraisal of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis; they are not validated or consensus-derived standards. Further empirical evaluation, stakeholder consultation, and consensus development are required.

Scientific researchers need reproducible software environments for complex applications that can run across heterogeneous computing platforms. Modern open source tools, like Pixi [1], provide automatic reproducibility solutions for all dependencies while providing a high-level interface well suited for researchers. This poster will provide a practical overview of using Pixi to easily create scientific and artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) environments that benefit from hardware acceleration, across multiple machines and platforms. The focus will be on CUDA applications, such as machine learning frameworks, and CUDA-enabled research software [2-4]. As AI/ML becomes a modern part of the scientific toolkit, the need to have robustly reproducible scientific computing environments that support hardware acceleration, e.g. with CUDA, becomes more important. However, historically just installing a working CUDA environment on a single machine, let alone on multiple platforms with different requirements, could be a difficult task for non-experts. This led to many scientific machine learning workflows being reliably runnable on only particular machines, and, even worse, with environments that were not reproducible across time. With significant recent advancements by the NVIDIA open source team and the conda-forge open source community, the entire CUDA stack — from compilers to development libraries — is now distributed on conda-forge. This significantly reduces the overhead to install CUDA dependencies, but packaging and distribution of binaries alone does not solve the problem of reproducibility. With automatic multi-platform digest-level lock file support for all dependencies that are available on package indexes (like PyPI and conda-forge), highly efficient solving strategies, and high-level user interfaces, Pixi provides a missing piece to the scientific researcher toolkit. The technology allows researchers to easily specify the hardware acceleration requirements they have, multiple different computational environments needed for their experiments, and required software dependencies. They can then quickly solve for a multi-platform lock file of all the dependencies required, down to the compiler level. This makes it possible to have multiple hardware-accelerated environments defined that are able to run hardware-accelerated workflows across heterogeneous machines with different GPU types and CUDA compatibility. The poster will also cover practical recommendations for deployment of locked software environments into production computing environments on traditional batch computing systems (e.g. HTCondor, Slurm) as well as cloud-native computing systems (e.g. Kubernetes, commercial cloud instances) [5]. It will also provide examples and links to published resources that provide fully templated Linux container definition files for arbitrary Pixi workspaces and computing requirements.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support mathematics teaching, yet research examining its instructional effects and implementation conditions in primary and secondary schools remains fragmented. This study reviewed published research on AI-assisted mathematics teaching between 2022 and 2026. Relevant records were retrieved from the Web of Science database using topic searches for AI and mathematics education. Of 262 initially identified records, 44 studies met the stated inclusion criteria and were included in a thematic synthesis. Three principal research areas emerged: instructional effects, factors influencing effectiveness, and strategies for improvement. The reviewed studies generally reported favourable outcomes for students’ mathematics achievement, conceptual understanding, interest, motivation and classroom engagement, although some interventions produced limited or inconsistent benefits. AI tools also supported teachers’ lesson planning, resource preparation, assessment, learning diagnosis and instructional decision-making. Reported outcomes depended on teacher-related factors, including AI literacy, attitudes and pedagogical competencies; student-related factors, including self-regulation, digital literacy and interaction patterns; technological factors, particularly accuracy, usability and personalisation; and contextual factors, including infrastructure, family support and educational resources. Suggested improvements included professional development, teacher-led implementation, clearer ethical and data-governance arrangements, and the development of more reliable mathematics-specific tools. The findings indicate that AI can provide useful instructional support, but its effectiveness depends on appropriate educational integration and local conditions. Longitudinal classroom research is needed to clarify sustained outcomes and the interaction of these factors.

documents.abstract: Adequate bowel preparation is the single most important determinant of colonoscopy quality, yet suboptimal preparation affects up to one-quarter of colonoscopies, leading to repeat procedures, increased health-system costs, and health disparities. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on bowel preparation regimens through a public health lens, organized around four interconnected dimensions: cleansing efficacy, safety, tolerability, and population-specific applicability. We define and classify preparation regimens by volume (high-volume ≥4 L, low-volume 2–<4 L, ultra-low-volume <2 L) and administration schedule (split-dose, same-day). Low-volume, split-dose formulations achieve non-inferior cleansing efficacy to high-volume 4L polyethylene glycol (PEG) regimens, with improved patient tolerability and compliance. The Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) is the most widely adopted assessment instrument; commonly used adequate preparation is defined as total BBPS ≥6 with each segment ≥2, although definitions vary across studies. PEG-based preparations maintain the most favorable safety profile, particularly in patients with renal or cardiovascular comorbidities, while sodium phosphate carries a small but clinically significant risk of acute phosphate nephropathy. Special populations—including older adults with frailty and polypharmacy, patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and those with diabetes—require tailored preparation strategies. Emerging evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), linaclotide, simethicone, dietary optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based bowel preparation assessment is critically evaluated. Health system implications, including the impact of inadequate preparation on resource utilization, adherence barriers linked to health literacy, and equity considerations, are examined. The review concludes that no single regimen is universally optimal; personalized preparation strategies integrating risk stratification, AI-assisted quality assessment, and evidence-based adjunctive protocols represent the most promising path toward improving colonoscopy outcomes at the population level.

Tuberculosis (TB), driven by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a leading cause of mortality from infectious disease worldwide.​ The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains—coupled with protracted treatment regimens and the persistence of latent infection—has not only compromised first-line chemotherapies but also underscored the stagnation of conventional drug development pipelines. In this review, we systematically synthesize how multi-scale computational strategies are reshaping anti-TB drug discovery and explicitly delineate their hierarchical integration—a cohesive framework that, to our knowledge, has yet to be comprehensively mapped in the existing literature.​ We survey four interconnected computational layers: (i) systems and network pharmacology for macroscopic target and pathway prioritization; (ii) machine learning (ML) for mesoscopic virtual screening, resistance classification, and ADMET prediction; (iii) molecular docking for microscopic elucidation of ligand–target binding modes; and (iv) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for atomic-level validation of binding poses and assessment of complex stability. Representative studies demonstrate that this workflow has pinpointed pivotal TB vulnerabilities (e.g., MmpL3, InhA, DprE1, ATP synthase, and FtsZ), enabled ML models to predict drug resistance from genomic data with high fidelity, and identified promising candidates such as vazabitide A (predicted binding affinity of −85.8 kcal/mol against Pks13) alongside repurposed agents (e.g., aldoxorubicin, quarfloxin). Critically, these computational predictions are reinforced by orthogonal experimental validation spanning in vitro enzymatic and phenotypic assays, in vivo infection models, clinical pharmacokinetic profiling, and multi-omics corroboration. We conclude that the top-down pipeline-spanning network pharmacology to ML, docking, and MD-integrated with bottom-up feedback constitutes a closed-loop paradigm that accelerates lead identification while addressing emergent drug resistance.​ Nevertheless, inherent limitations in predictive reliability and cross-layer error propagation necessitate rigorous downstream experimental validation. Looking forward, generative artificial intelligence, self-driving laboratories, and standardized cross-method benchmarking are poised to consolidate this multi-scale pipeline into a robust engine for next-generation anti-TB therapeutics.
topics: Synthesis and Characterization of Heterocyclic Compounds

documents.abstract: Background: We explored which point of care (POC) resources medical residents at the University at Buffalo use in clinical settings. We specifically sought to gather feedback from residents who help train medical students to see how they discover, use, and promote resources to support patient care. Case Presentation: We developed an eight question Qualtrics survey. Residency program coordinators emailed the survey to approximately 445 residents in the following programs: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Combined Internal Medicine and Pediatrics, Neurology, Child Neurology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, Surgery, Plastic Surgery, and Vascular Surgery. The programs we targeted all correspond to required clerkship rotations. The survey was open for two weeks in June 2025. Thirty-nine residents (8.8%) completed our survey. Thirty-five, or nearly 90% of respondents, reported that they frequently use UpToDate, followed by twenty-three (59.0%) that use OpenEvidence, and seventeen that use MDCalc (43.6%). The residents we surveyed were inclined to recommend similar resources to medical students. They most often hear about new resources from other residents and attendings, via announcements on social media or podcasts, or by attending grand rounds and conferences. Conclusions: Our results highlight the continued popularity of UpToDate among medical trainees but also suggest that residents frequently use OpenEvidence in clinical settings. Further studies are needed to determine the impact of artificial intelligence tools on patient care and learning outcomes.

Agentic artificial intelligence combines goal-directed reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, adaptation and multi-agent coordination with the ability to affect external systems. This capability raises problems of authorization, safety, human oversight, accountability and the evidence required to justify reliance. This non-systematic integrative survey distinguishes AI ethics, responsible AI, governance, trustworthiness, assurance, explainability, security and controllability; synthesizes preventive, detective, corrective, human-based and agent-based controls; and compares responsibility and oversight arrangements across the agent lifecycle. Building on established governance and meaningful-human-control research, it proposes an authority-control-assurance-accountability mapping that connects normative requirements to delegated decision rights, enforceable controls, observable evidence, escalation conditions and identifiable organizational owners. Two fictional cases illustrate the proposed mapping for document access and software changes. The framework is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirically validated assurance standard. The survey identifies limitations of supervisory-agent independence, long-horizon explanation, dynamic authorization and continuous re-assurance, and specifies research questions for future evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Team situation awareness (SA) is essential for effective team performance. Yet, current methods rely on potentially biased self-reports and obtrusive tools such as task probes. Objective, unobtrusive, and continuous methods for monitoring team SA could support its improvement. In contrast to individual SA, unobtrusive measures of team SA have not been systematically reviewed. Because team SA is an umbrella concept, we adapted a framework proposed by Salmon et al., identifying two components that can potentially be measured unobtrusively: shared mental models (SMMs) and team coordination. This systematic review examines behavioural and physiological technologies that may enable unobtrusive measurement of these components. Methods We conducted a systematic literature review of studies investigating behavioural technologies, such as verbal communication and eye-tracking, and physiological technologies, such as electroencephalography, for unobtrusive measurement of team SMMs and coordination. We searched Web of Science (May and July 2025) for relevant literature published between 2000 and 2025. We included peer-reviewed articles published in English. In total, 19 studies addressing team SMMs and 33 addressing team coordination were included. We extracted sample and team size, task environment, operationalisation of team SMMs and coordination, and their relationship with unobtrusive measures. Results Cardiac measures (42%) and verbal communication (47%) were most popular for estimating team SMMs, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (27%) and cardiac measures (30%) were most popular for estimating team coordination. Interpersonal synchrony—the temporal contiguity and interdependence of physiological and/or behavioural activity between teammates—was applied in 70% of team coordination studies. Studies covered diverse tasks and settings, from laboratory-based cognitive tasks and controlled physical tasks to real-world environments, including surgery. Various methods were used to operationalise SMMs and coordination, including participant experience, expert assessment, and self-reports. Discussion Findings suggest that team SMMs and coordination cannot be measured as single, unified constructs using one unobtrusive measure. Instead, different measures may provide information about specific aspects of these processes. Future research should begin with task analysis to identify relevant aspects of team SA and derive appropriate measures for the specific task environment. Task-related behavioural actions also represent a potentially valuable, yet often overlooked, category of unobtrusive measures. A key limitation is the substantial variation in how SMMs and coordination were operationalised and measured, making direct comparisons difficult. Future work should investigate how identified measures relate directly to team SA using validated measures.

Water is crucial for rice growth, particularly in semi-arid Australia, where climate change threatens water allocation for rice growers and challenges the sustainability of the rice industry. Estimating water depth using remote sensing can be beneficial, as it can help growers transition from traditional continuous flooding (CF) to irrigation practices such as Delayed Permanent Water (DPW) and Aerobic Rice (AR), which are promising pathways to ensure industry sustainability. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has been widely evaluated for water depth prediction in rice crops. To date, a significant gap remains in the performance of the proposed models, with authors suggesting the use of optical and SAR data to improve their estimates. To this end, this research evaluated three machine learning (ML) models to estimate water depth in rice under different irrigation practices in the Australian semi-arid region. Three different ML approaches (Tree-based, Neural Networks, and pretrained foundational model) were evaluated with three data configurations: Set 1 with SAR only, set 2 with Optical Only, and Set 3 with multimodal (SAR and Optical) data. The pre-trained foundational model achieved the best results, with RMSE of 14.19 cm, MAE of 10.01 cm, R2 of 0.63, KGE of 0.73, and CCC of 0.78. Interestingly, the SHAP analysis reveals that optical remote sensing is more significant for the model than SAR. Specifically, the mean GVMI and VAWIlog standard deviation.

Macrovascular complications are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Early risk identification and accurate risk stratification are essential for both primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention. With the rapid development of electronic health records, medical imaging, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI), risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications have evolved from traditional statistical approaches to machine learning-, deep learning-, and multimodal AI-driven models. However, despite substantial improvements in predictive performance, current models remain limited by heterogeneous target populations, inconsistent outcome definitions, insufficient external validation, limited clinical interpretability, and inadequate real-world implementation, thereby restricting their clinical translation. This review summarizes the evolution, data sources, modeling methodologies, clinical applications, and future perspectives of risk prediction models for macrovascular complications in T2DM. We first describe the transition from conventional cardiovascular risk scores, including the Framingham Risk Score, to diabetes-specific models such as the UKPDS Risk Engine, ADVANCE, RECODe, and SCORE2-Diabetes, followed by the emergence of AI-based prediction models. We then review the major data sources used in contemporary prediction models, including clinical characteristics, laboratory biomarkers, vascular function and imaging, multi-omics profiles, and wearable device-derived data. Furthermore, we compare the strengths and limitations of traditional statistical methods, machine learning, deep learning, and multitask learning with respect to predictive performance, interpretability, and clinical applicability, and discuss the major challenges related to study design, external validation, data quality, algorithmic bias, and real-world implementation. Finally, we propose that future risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications will evolve from single-source data to multimodal data integration, from static risk estimation to dynamic risk trajectories, from single outcomes to multiple interconnected cardiovascular outcomes, from prognosis prediction to individualized treatment benefit prediction, and from standalone algorithms to continuously learning clinical decision support systems. Emerging technologies, including foundation models, large language models, digital twins, causal inference, and continuous learning frameworks, are expected to drive the transition from Risk Prediction to Clinical Decision and ultimately Patient Benefit, thereby advancing precision prevention and individualized management of diabetes.

The current pace of urbanization has imposed unprecedented strains on transport, water, energy and housing networks and the smart city paradigm has become the key policy response. However, the effectiveness of smart city programmes rely more on the construction management (CM) systems involved in planning, coordination and delivery of the physical infrastructure underpinning smart city programmes. The literature reviewed in the following paper is divided into six themes: smart city concept and smart city components; core functions of CM (planning, scheduling, cost, quality and safety); digital tools (Building Information Modelling (BIM), Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI)); lean and sustainable construction; risk management, stakeholder management, public–private partnership (PPP); and field evidence from smart city Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. The results of the synthesis indicate that the use of BIM-based coordination in the project reduced the number of design errors from 25 to 8 and rework cost by 64%, while lean JIT delivery reduced material waste by 60-67% and smart building systems reduced the energy demand by 40%. The adaptive traffic control in Sagar reduced junction delay by 37.5 %; sensorbased LED street lighting reduced connected load by 52 % and the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) reduced complaint response by 75 %. Financial risk (20/25) and inter-agency coordination (20/25) were identified as the main barriers. A challenge–strategy framework and an agenda of future research are suggested on digital twins, AI-assisted scheduling and capacity building.

The rapid transformation of higher education in the digital age has introduced online advising as a central pillar of student support. Online advising encompasses the deployment of digital communication platforms, learning management systems (LMS), artificial intelligence tools, and data analytics to guide, mentor, and support students through their academic journeys. This chapter provides a comprehensive, evidence-based examination of the principal barriers to effective online advising in higher education. The chapter identifies and analyses six major barrier domains: (1) technological infrastructure and digital divide challenges; (2) the deficit of personalised interaction; (3) communication and linguistic challenges; (4) inadequate advisor training and professional development; (5) institutional policy and structural constraints; and (6) data privacy, security, and ethical governance concerns. For each barrier domain, the chapter presents empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, illustrative data and practical case examples to ground the analysis.

SÆLQIR-M1 investigates compressed neural-network weights as directly executable memory, combining an exact finite-field compiler with a digital near-memory architecture. The objective is to reduce repeated computation and weight movement in AI inference while developing a practical extension to GPU-centered computing systems. This release includes a 78-page technical manuscript, mathematical proofs, executable software, packed memory formats, independent native references, hardware design candidates, experimental records, and a staged prototype-validation plan. The central mechanism is exact shared-character compilation. Structured weight tiles represent integer operators through binary parity characters, finite coefficients, and a scatter-Walsh-gather computation. The compiler determines whether tiles using different internal coordinate maps can share one input scatter and Walsh–Hadamard transform without changing their decoded integer weights. It factors the centered sign patterns of active terms over GF(2); their rank gives the minimum common label dimension within the declared character-preserving representation family. Admission also enforces finite coefficient ranges, compatible scales and epochs, and hardware resource limits. For four compatible 64×64 tiles, the released example reduces complete framed storage from 4,352 to 3,968 bytes-an 8.8235% reduction-and counted serial work from 6,144 to 4,224 cycles-a 31.25% reduction. The number of Walsh transforms decreases from four to one, with no additional approximation introduced by sharing. These cycle counts describe a reference schedule; they are not measured GPU speedups. Incompatible groups remain separate. The original software evidence comprises 200 passing Python tests, 18 exact independent C++ FORK cases, six exact C++ D4 cases, and successful compiled C loader and driver checks. A small architecture-trained handwritten-digit classifier demonstrates packed execution: all 270 held-out integer output vectors match the pre-sharing dense reference, with 263/270 correct classifications. The scalar INT4 comparator achieves 264/270 correct classifications but worse negative log-likelihood. Both outcomes are retained; this experiment establishes executable-format correctness, not general model-quality superiority. The proposed FORK engine places arithmetic beside ordinary digital SRAM. Its contract supports 64 signed INT8 inputs, up to 256 output rows, four signed INT16 coefficients per row, six-bit character labels, 16-bit scratch storage, and 40-bit held outputs. A complementary generic INT4-weight/INT8-activation path addresses matrices outside the structured family, although its integration remains incomplete. The system proposal retains CPU, GPU, shared DRAM, storage, and operating-system functions, with executable-weight engines serving eligible AI operations. The release is a pre-silicon research prototype. It contains no completed HDL simulation, synthesis, FPGA measurement, fabricated ASIC, or matched modern-LLM/GPU benchmark. Cost and throughput scenarios are explicitly identified as assumptions or planning calculations. The practical research opportunity is to connect compact operator representations, exact transform sharing, compiler admission criteria, and memory-local execution. The decisive next steps are to measure eligibility in useful pretrained models and determine whether storage and scheduled-work savings survive configuration, transfers, refill traffic, fallback execution, and physical hardware constraints. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) have achieved rapid technological advancement, yet their widespread adoption has introduced new and multifaceted safety challenges. This review provides a systematic synthesis of ADAS-related accident scenarios and risk factors. Based on multinational accident databases and detailed crash reports, collision types are classified into three major categories: vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-pedestrian, and vehicle-to-non-motorized interactions. The underlying causes of these accidents are traced to sensor performance degradation under adverse weather, algorithmic limitations in dynamic traffic environments, and excessive driver dependence on automated functions. Furthermore, this review examines mainstream analytical approaches, including statistical modeling, system-theoretic frameworks, and AI-driven techniques, and evaluates their applicability in risk identification and mitigation. Finally, a forward-looking framework is proposed to advance multi-sensor data fusion and privacy-preserving governance, strengthen dynamic scene modeling and open scenario databases, and incorporate human factors into causal inference for proactive risk management. The findings are expected to enrich the methodological foundation of ADAS accident analysis and support future improvements in intelligent vehicle safety.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This thesis examines the scientific and methodological foundations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational processes under digital transformation. Drawing on research in information systems, organizational AI readiness, software engineering, and risk management, it identifies the conditions under which AI adoption can generate measurable value. The analysis distinguishes technological deployment from organizational transformation and considers data governance, model selection, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring as interdependent implementation requirements. A conceptual, stage-based approach is proposed for connecting organizational objectives with technical design and operational performance. The contribution is methodological and analytical; no independent experimental outcomes or unverified performance improvements are claimed.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to address the information security governance issues associated with the use of AI in HRM by developing the artificial intelligence–human resource management (AI-HRM) cybersecurity architecture (AHCA), a novel domain-specific architecture. Design/methodology/approach The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles, and 72 peer-reviewed papers were obtained from journals indexed in Scopus and IEEE Xplore, or from CORE-ranked journals, for the years 2020–2025, with citation chaining in Google Scholar. Three research questions guided the synthesis, covering threat conceptualisation, security implications and governance. This study then created the AHCA following an iterative design science process, using each component directly from literature reviews, and constructed a structured rubric with explicit anchoring examples to enable replication of the comparative evaluation. Findings The review identified six categories of AI-HRM security threats: data breaches (T1), exploitation of algorithmic bias (T2), insider threat amplification (T3), model poisoning attacks (T4), regulatory non-compliance (T5) and governance and audit failures (T6). There is a wide disparity in the attention these subjects receive in the literature: algorithmic bias (43.1 %) and governance and audit failure (51.4 %) together account for 94.4 % of the corpus whose primary focus could be coded, while data breaches (1.4 %), insider threat (1.4 %) and regulatory non-compliance (2.8 %) sit at the margins, and no study takes model poisoning as its primary focus. In addition, most governance-oriented research identifies accountability gaps but stops short of architectural solutions. The AHCA is designed to address this structural deficit, pairing four-layer architecture with a 14-indicator security performance indicator (SPI) framework. Research limitations/implications The corpus is limited to English-language publications from 2020 to 2025 that appear in journals in the AHCA’s Q1 or Q2 tiers, and the AHCA itself is a design artefact that will be tested in practice through Delphi panels of experts and longitudinal case studies. The technical security literature emerged when searching IEEE Xplore and Scopus; a complementary search of the ACM Digital Library is planned as a future extension. Practical implications The AHCA and its SPI framework offer HR practitioners and policymakers an AI-HRM-specific blueprint for general data protection regulation (GDPR) compliant, high-risk employment systems in accordance with the provisions of the European Union AI Act. Originality/value The AHCA incorporates GDPR and EU AI Act compliance-by-design principles into a single HRM-specific security architecture that is currently in the early phases of development. It is the only benchmark that addresses the HRM-specific and EU AI Act dimensions, which are not addressed by sector-agnostic comparators, and it performs well in the generic HRM security dimensions on a replicable nine-dimension rubric, benchmarked against NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, ISO 27001 and NIST CSF.

documents.abstract: Objective To investigate the self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in pediatric healthcare in a children’s specialty hospital, and to compare differences between the two groups. Methods This single-center cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted at Fujian Children’s Hospital from January 2026 to June 2026. A self-designed questionnaire was used to assess healthcare workers’ and caregivers’ self-reported understanding, trust, risk perception, and willingness to accept AI applications in pediatric healthcare. Respondents were divided into groups according to their identity. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, while continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Results A total of 261 respondents were included, comprising 159 caregivers and 102 healthcare workers. Healthcare workers had a higher level of self-reported understanding and a higher frequency of use of AI applications in pediatric healthcare than caregivers ( p < 0.01); however, they also showed stronger perceptions of data security risks ( p < 0.001). Caregivers reported greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making than healthcare workers ( p < 0.001). Most respondents believed that AI could not replace pediatric healthcare workers, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups ( p = 0.166). Regarding potential advantages, healthcare workers were more likely to agree that AI could reduce human error ( p < 0.001). Regarding potential limitations, healthcare workers expressed greater concern about the risks of misdiagnosis, lack of humanistic care, and data privacy and security issues ( p < 0.001). Conclusion In this single-center children’s specialty hospital, healthcare workers reported greater self-rated understanding and more frequent use of AI, together with stronger awareness of several potential risks, whereas caregivers showed greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making despite lower self-rated understanding. These findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger multicenter studies before being generalized to broader populations in China.

The speakers discussed a range of techniques and insights into how safety engineers might benefit from the use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Large Language Models (LLMs), examining everything from prompt engineering to building applications and custom tools from AI code generators.

documents.abstract: The full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, which began in February 2022, caused acute and long-term disruptions in the activities of Ukrainian companies, forcing them to quickly rebuild their organizational structures, decision-making mechanisms, and planning practices. This article offers a conceptual and analytical explanation of how wartime conditions accelerated the transition from centralised management measures to cross-functional crisis teams, shared leadership mechanisms and emerging learning operating models. This study is based on secondary data analysis and illustrative case studies, rather than original empirical research. It combines business survey data, institutional and corporate reports, and academic literature. On this basis, the article outlines an organizational trajectory from centralization to distributed cross-functional decision-making and beyond to what this study defines as a learning operating model. The article also highlights that AI-enabled practices (including situational dashboards, scenario modeling, demand forecasting, and knowledge management) supported by generative AI can accelerate collective situational awareness in wartime. However, role overload and coordination burdens can also increase in the absence of clarity of purpose. Thus, shared leadership in the study is viewed as potentially “a dual-effect organizational mechanism”. The conclusions outline the implications for Ukrainian business practices and compare the identified trajectories of organizational response of Ukrainian companies with future constraints associated with the European model of AI governance. This paper addresses a gap in the literature by establishing a link among shared leadership, contingency planning, and AI-based situational analysis in the specific context of business resilience in wartime. And its practical contribution is to identify organizational conditions under which AI tools can support distributed decision making without increasing coordination overhead.

Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

Collecting diverse real-world data for AI model training is often costly, time-consuming, and constrained by safety and experimental conditions, making simulation environments an important alternative for data collection. However, existing methods for generating simulation environments often rely on predefined asset libraries and provide limited support for integrating user-specific personas. This paper proposes a persona-aware pipeline for generating 3D desk simulation environments based on a user persona defined by an occupation and Big Five personality traits. Given the input persona, an LLM generates structured scene layout information and an image generation model produces a synthetic desk image, followed by library-free 3D asset reconstruction using SAM 2 for object segmentation and SAM 3D for object-level 3D reconstruction. The assets are then rendered in Isaac Sim using grid mapping and scene graph-based spatial relationships. Experimental results show that persona variables produce interpretable changes in object composition and workspace atmosphere. Qualitative rendering results further show that the proposed pipeline can transfer the layout structure of a target image into a simulation environment, demonstrating its potential for generating diverse and controllable persona-aware simulation environments.

Computer vision and artificial intelligence allow the development of novel methods of posture evaluation in health and training. This paper describes a MediaPipe-based system that identifies hand gestures using 21 landmarks and provides accurate feedback. With 92 percent accuracy in multiple conditions, its light design makes it versatile, secure, and accessible during the therapy and training process. This is the outlining succinctly of the workflow: acquisition of inputs, landmarks with the MediaPipe, angles and distance features, machine learning classification, and real-time feedback generation. This brief supplement explains methodology as well as applications and results.

The Smart Crop Advisory System is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to assist farmers in making informed farming decisions. Traditional agriculture faces several challenges, including unsuitable crop selection, unpredictable weather conditions, crop diseases, and fluctuations in market prices. The proposed system integrates essential agricultural services, including crop recommendation, weather forecasting, crop disease detection, agricultural market price information, and an AI-based multilingual voice assistant. It also provides farmer profile management, crop price trend analysis, and rainfall trend visualization through an interactive dashboard. The crop recommendation module helps farmers identify suitable crops based on relevant agricultural parameters, while the disease detection module supports the identification of potential crop diseases. Weather and market information help farmers plan agricultural activities and make informed selling decisions. The multilingual voice assistant aims to improve accessibility by enabling farmers to interact with the system through voice-based communication. Overall, the Smart Crop Advisory System aims to improve access to agricultural information, support effective decision-making, promote efficient resource utilization, and encourage sustainable farming practices. Keywords: Smart Agriculture, Crop Recommendation, Machine Learning, Crop Disease Detection, Weather Forecasting, Market Price Analysis, Voice Assistant, Sustainable Agriculture.

As social media and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning and daily lives, fatigue arising from established digital platforms and anxiety surrounding emerging AI may constitute interrelated forms of technology-related distress. However, how these experiences are jointly associated with depressive symptoms, and whether these associations vary by subjective socioeconomic status (SSES), remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and research on status maintenance, this cross-sectional study examined AI anxiety as a statistical mediator of the association between social media fatigue and depressive symptoms and further tested whether SSES moderated the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms. Survey data from 1108 Chinese university students were analyzed using regression models with heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3 (HC3) robust standard errors and percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals. Social media fatigue was positively associated with AI anxiety, which in turn was positively associated with depressive symptoms, yielding a significant statistical indirect association. As SSES increased, the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms became stronger, and the corresponding conditional indirect association also increased. Overall, these findings suggest that understanding university students’ digital mental health requires attention to both distress arising across different technological environments and the subjective social positions from which these experiences are evaluated, offering a more context-sensitive perspective on how established and emerging forms of digital stress may be jointly associated with psychological well-being.

Sovereign OS v200 formalises a behavioural‑systems organisational diagnostic architecture capable of reading modern organisations as multi‑layer, multi‑domain, multi‑reality ecosystems. Building on the emergence of human–AI co‑processing documented in the Sovereign Cognition whitepaper, v200 integrates behavioural insight, cognitive altitude, and long‑context reasoning to produce a unified diagnostic model that neither human practitioners nor AI systems could generate independently. The architecture provides whole‑system organisational clarity by distinguishing between formal, informal, stated, lived, and emerging realities while tracing behavioural drift across cultural, operational, financial, compliance, strategic, and technical domains. v200 introduces consolidated diagnostic artefacts—including Whole‑System Maps, Coherence Frames, Integration Maps, Stability Indices, and Reality Alignment Frames—that detect instability long before traditional data sources reveal symptoms. Designed for complex, politically sensitive, multi‑stakeholder, and legacy‑constrained environments, Sovereign OS v200 establishes a new cognitive discipline for organisational diagnostics. It demonstrates how human–AI co‑processing can stabilise ecosystems, align realities, and support altitude‑based consulting across modern organisational landscapes.

This article examines the role of psychological resilience and emotional self- regulation in enhancing athletes’ competitive performance. In sporting environments characterized by psychological pressure, pre-competition anxiety, unexpected setbacks, and high performance expectations, the ability to maintain psychological balance becomes particularly important. The article explores psychological resilience in relation to adapting to challenging situations, recovering from defeat, and sustaining intrinsic motivation. It also discusses the contribution of emotional self-regulation to attentional control, the management of impulsive reactions, and effective decision-making during competitions. Particular emphasis is placed on approaches to strengthening athletes’ psychological stability through specialized training exercises, individualized psychological support, and the development of self-regulation skills. These approaches may help improve athletes’ psychological preparedness and enable them to demonstrate their abilities more effectively under competitive conditions.

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is concerned with how intelligence agents take actions in a given environment to maximize the cumulative reward they receive. In healthcare, applying RL algorithms could assist patients in improving their health status. In ride-sharing platforms, applying RL algorithms could increase drivers’ income and customer satisfaction. For large language models, applying RL algorithms could align their outputs with human preferences. Over the past decade, RL has been arguably one of the most vibrant research frontiers in machine learning. Nevertheless, statistics as a field, as opposed to computer science, has only recently begun to engage with RL both in depth and in breadth. This chapter presents a selective review of statistical inferential tools for RL, covering both hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction. Our goal is to highlight the value of statistical inference in RL for both the statistics and machine learning communities, and to promote the broader application of classical statistical inference tools in this vibrant area of research.

Digital transformation has changed the way organizations manage human resources, particularly in identifying, developing, placing, and retaining talent. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in talent management enables organizations to utilize data to support recruitment, competency mapping, employee development, career planning, performance evaluation, and talent retention. This article aims to analyze strategies for building AI-based talent by reviewing eight articles related to artificial intelligence, talent management, human resource development, talent acquisition, and data integration. This study uses a literature review approach by comparing the findings, research focuses, methods, benefits, and challenges discussed in the selected sources. The literature indicates that AI can support organizations in identifying talent and employee potential, analyzing competency gaps, providing personalized learning programs, supporting career development, and predicting employee turnover risks. However, AI implementation also presents challenges, including algorithmic bias, data quality limitations, lack of transparency, privacy concerns, organizational readiness, and the need for digital competencies. Therefore, an AI-based talent development strategy should integrate technology, data quality, organizational readiness, leadership, employee development, and ethical governance. AI should complement human judgment rather than replace the human role in talent management. This collaboration can improve talent management while maintaining contextual, relational, and ethical considerations.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing organizational strategy, decision-making, resource allocation, and operational coordination. As AI moves from task automation and analytical support toward generative systems and intelligent agents, its role is expanding across organizational functions. AI-orchestrated organizations integrate AI capabilities with human expertise to support information analysis, opportunity identification, decision support, workflow coordination, and learning. This creates opportunities for greater strategic responsiveness, while also raising issues of decision authority, accountability, governance, and organizational control. This study examines AI orchestration through a dynamic capabilities perspective and develops a conceptual framework linking AI-enabled sensing, strategic seizing, resource reconfiguration, human–AI coordination, governance, and continuous learning. The framework positions AI as an enabling organizational capability rather than an isolated technological resource and emphasizes the interaction between technological capabilities, human judgement, organizational resources, and governance. It further explains how these elements can support strategic responsiveness, organizational agility, and continuous adaptation as organizations respond to changing environments. The study develops seven conceptual propositions to provide a structured basis for future empirical examination of AI-orchestrated strategic management.

In 2025, the Centre for Interprofessional Workplace Learning (TVEPS) co-designed a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) with partners from Denmark, Sweden, and Norway as part of a NordPlus project. The aim was for students from different disciplines and countries to become agents of change for grand societal challenges through collaboration on wicked problems in a workshop with representatives from municipalities and educational institutions. Exploring real-life wicked problems without straightforward solutions can enable students, municipalities, and scientific staff to create social, environmental, and economic value and to contribute to the fulfilment of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, including the provision of ethical and responsible healthcare services. The workshop comprised two parts: an online week and a one-week on-site challenge workshop at Chalmers University of Technology. Stockholm, Sweden. The students were introduced to grand societal challenges from the municipalities of Øygarden (Norway), Kolding (Denmark), and Aarhus (Denmark). Their task was to explore wicked problems in interprofessional teams comprising students from health, social care, engineering, design, and entrepreneurship disciplines, using an innovation process to identify sustainable opportunities and hypotheses that could later be investigated, developed, and implemented in collaboration with the municipalities. During the challenge workshop, the student teams engaged in close dialogue with municipal representatives, experts in municipal economics, and facilitators from the educational institutions. Educational institutions derived significant benefits from the interprofessional, cross-sectoral, Nordic teaching format. Students gained valuable insight through reflection and close collaboration, developing innovative perspectives, potential opportunities, and hypotheses related to the societal challenges presented. These can be further developed and implemented to benefit the participating municipalities, whose representatives received input of potentially high societal value.

This study explored the lived experiences of Grade 12 Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) students in using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for learning Social Studies in Malapatan III District, Schools Division of Sarangani, Philippines. Anchored in Moustakas’ Transcendental Phenomenology, Davis’ Technology Acceptance Model, and Zimmerman’s Self-Regulated Learning Theory, the study employed a qualitative phenomenological research design. Nine Grade 12 HUMSS students from three public secondary schools participated in in-depth interviews, while three Social Studies teachers participated in a focus group discussion for data triangulation. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, and data were gathered using a validated semi-structured interview guide and analyzed thematically. The findings identified twelve emerging themes encompassing students’ lived experiences, the contexts shaping AI-supported learning, and their perspectives on future AI integration. Participants perceived AI as a valuable learning resource that improved conceptual understanding, academic productivity, confidence, classroom engagement, and emotional well-being. However, excessive dependence, reduced independent thinking, information accuracy, and academic integrity emerged as significant concerns. Students emphasized the importance of responsible AI use, critical evaluation, and continued teacher guidance. The study recommends strengthening AI literacy, ethical practices, and teacher capacity building through the proposed Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration and Learning Empowerment Program (RAILEP). The findings primarily support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting responsible, inclusive, and learner-centered technology integration. The study contributes to educational and institutional sustainability by informing school-based guidelines and instructional practices that balance technological innovation with academic integrity, learner autonomy, and meaningful human interaction.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in mitigating online financial fraud among women, analyzing survey data from 75 respondents. The demographic profile is heavily skewed toward younger, digital-native generations, with 92% of respondents aged 18–35 and nearly half (46.7%) identifying as students. This sample exhibits high digital integration, with 73.3% utilizing digital payment applications daily. Concurrently, risk exposure is pervasive: 89.3% are aware of online cybercrimes, and 74.7% have direct or secondary experience with financial scams—predominantly fake loan apps, UPI fraud, and OTP scams. Consequently, 69.3% express deep anxiety regarding transaction safety. To counteract these threats, respondents strongly endorse technological intervention. General AI literacy is high at 70.7%, and 68% recognize AI’s current application in banking security. Optimism regarding its efficacy is robust: 70.7% believe AI can significantly reduce financial fraud targeting women, primarily because 74.7% trust it to detect threats faster than human operators. To establish a sense of security, users demand proactive, real-time defenses rather than passive analysis, heavily prioritizing instant fraud alerts (37.3%), background transaction monitoring, and automated transaction blocking. Ultimately, 72% of respondents demand that banking institutions escalate AI security integration. However, the data highlights that technology alone is insufficient; an overwhelming 78.7% emphasize that robust AI deployment must be paired with comprehensive financial literacy and grassroots cybersecurity awareness campaigns. This dual strategy of advanced technological defense and target user education is deemed essential to safely empower women within the digital economy.

Purpose This study assesses the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) among entrepreneurs in Spain, examining both sufficient and necessary conditions for different levels of use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses survey data from the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas. Ordered logistic regression is applied to identify sufficient conditions, while Necessary Condition Analysis is used to detect bottlenecks for higher levels of GenAI use. Findings Knowledge of GenAI and perceived economic usefulness are the main predictors of more intensive use. However, the NCA shows that technological optimism and the absence of very high scepticism operate as necessary conditions, especially at regular levels of use. Research limitations/implications The assessment relies on cross-sectional, self-reported data from Spanish self-employed workers. Future research should distinguish between different entrepreneurial profiles and types of GenAI use. The analytical framework may be applicable across different contexts, although the specific associations and bottleneck thresholds observed here should be validated through cross-country research. Practical implications Support policies should combine awareness-raising, applied training, and practical guidance on how GenAI can generate value in entrepreneurial activity. Social implications The findings suggest that responsible GenAI adoption among entrepreneurs requires not only favourable attitudes towards technology but also knowledge, perceived usefulness, and clear guidance on its business applications. Originality/value The study contributes by combining sufficiency and necessity logics to explain actual GenAI use among entrepreneurs, rather than focussing only on behavioural intention, while indicating that technology-readiness dispositions and GenAI-specific behavioural factors may fulfil distinct roles at different levels of use. By distinguishing probabilistic drivers from necessary bottlenecks, the study provides a more complete account of entrepreneurial GenAI adoption and generates more actionable implications for training and policies aimed at increasing effective use.

documents.abstract: Synmanitik Band 2: 200 deutsch-englische Arbeitsdefinitionen zu sachbezogenen Rückfragen, dokumentierten Annahmen und kontrollierter Umsetzung wissenschaftlicher Dokumentinhalte. Alle Einträge sind Bereichsfestlegungen. Beispiele, Gegenfälle und Grenzen stehen auf Deutsch. Zehn Module behandeln Rückfragen, Auftragsbezug, Befunde, Vorschläge, Änderungen, Zustände, Dokumentanmerkungen, Protokolle, Rückmeldungsumsetzung und Ausgabegrenzen. Der Band setzt eigene Vorarbeiten fort; er ist keine bestätigte Disziplingründung, historische Neuheitsbestätigung oder gemessene Kooperationswirkung. Mit KI-Unterstützung ausgearbeitete und redaktionell geprüfte Arbeitsfassung. Volume 2 contains 200 paired German-English scoped working definitions. Supporting examples and boundaries are in German. Original standard-library synthetic cases distinguish a proposed note from an implemented field correction, a correct field change from an unwanted change to protected content, and a current finding from a stale positive finding. A short ASCII text case demonstrates positional anchor drift after insertion and rejects a mismatching version. Two fixed event sequences are checked under an explicitly stipulated ordering rule. The use of synthetic data is becoming increasingly widespread in a variety of applications. For hate speech detection, synthetic data offers the chance to overcome limitations of existing models and datasets, such as data scarcity, negative psychological impact on annotators, and privacy issues. However, previous work on the topic has only focused on evaluating synthetic datasets extrinsically, by measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic texts. In this work, in addition to measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic data in cross-distribution setups, we carry out a qualitative analysis, aiming at assessing how closely synthetic data can mimic authentic user-generated and human-annotated data. We focus in particular on possible issues related to (under)representation of specific minority groups as targets of hate in synthetic data. To do this, we augment an existing English hate speech dataset by paraphrasing the original gold data using three large language models, and then evaluate the synthetic data both quantitatively, including testing out-of-distribution model generalization, and qualitatively, examining the realism of synthetic texts, their hate speech content, and whether they represent the same identity groups as the original data. We pair this analysis with a detailed breakdown, for each demographic characteristic, of how the synthetic data creation process affects the representation of each specific type of identity, which is the main contribution of our work. We find that, while the performance of models trained on synthetic data is promising, these texts are easily identified as written by an LLM by humans, hate speech labels are not necessarily preserved, and the paraphrasing process tends to erase representation of minority groups and intersectional identities, affecting certain demographics more than others.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing educational practices, introducing innovative approaches to teaching, learning, assessment, and classroom management. The successful implementation of AI in educational institutions largely depends on the preparation and acceptance of teachers, especially teacher trainers, who play a key role in training future teachers. This study examines the perceptions, perceptions, and readiness of bachelor's degree recipients in education. University teacher on the integration of artificial intelligence into school education. A descriptive survey design was used to collect data from 25 randomly selected undergraduate faculty members. Universities in Indore city were surveyed through a structured questionnaire. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis. The results showed that the majority of participants had a positive view of AI and recognized its potential to improve teaching effectiveness, support personalized learning, and reduce administrative burden on teachers. However, concerns related to ethical concerns, data privacy, inadequate training, and inadequate organizational infrastructure continue to impact teachers' readiness to adopt AI. The study recommends integrating an AI culture into teacher preparation programs, strengthening digital infrastructure, and organizing regular professional development efforts to effectively and responsibly integrate AI into educational environments. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Readiness, Teacher Education, AI Integration, Digital Competency.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes healthcare, public health and health professions education. However, predictive and generative systems can reproduce or amplify longstanding inequalities embedded in data, institutions and established knowledge structures. Public health education therefore needs to connect technical approaches to identifying and mitigating algorithmic bias with their broader social, population health and institutional contexts. This conceptual article presents the sociotechnical Bias literacy for public health education framework (SBL-PHE), developed through a theory-informed conceptual synthesis drawing on conceptual framework analysis. A focused supplementary literature search in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and the ACM digital library was conducted to examine and refine its theoretical foundations. An evidence-informed composite case of AI-supported cardiovascular risk assessment traces algorithmic gender bias from knowledge production and data representation through modeling and implementation to monitoring. The framework comprises five interconnected competency dimensions concerned with recognizing, explaining, evaluating, addressing and reflecting on algorithmic bias. For master’s-level public health education, these dimensions are linked to learning objectives, learning activities, assessment methods and a prospective evaluation strategy. Sociotechnical Bias literacy is proposed as a foundational competency for public health professionals who use or interpret AI. Sociotechnical fluency describes an advanced, role-dependent capability, particularly for responsibilities in implementation, evaluation, translation and governance. SBL-PHE provides a theoretically grounded framework for integrating technical understanding, health equity, professional judgment and institutional responsibility into public health education. The framework and its proposed educational application have not yet been empirically validated.
